video.title: Agents, environments and decisions: PEAS, MDPs and rewards
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Dr Salma - statistics lecturer, Cairo University (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A student trains a cleaning agent rewarded for each piece of dirt it picks up. It learns to drop dirt and pick it up again, forever. The code has no bug. What went wrong?
Today: the classical definition of an agent, how Markov decision processes model sequential choices, and why reward design is where student projects go wrong.

An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators. A rational agent chooses actions that maximise its expected performance measure. PEAS names the four things to specify: performance, environment, actuators and sensors.
An MDP has states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards. A policy maps each state to an action. The goal is the policy that maximises expected discounted return.
With a discount of zero point nine, a reward of ten arriving in two steps is worth eight point one now. Discounting makes sooner rewards worth more. It also keeps infinite sums finite.

The agent optimises exactly the reward you wrote, not the goal you meant. Rewarding pickups instead of a clean room invites the loop. This is called specification gaming, and it happens in real systems.

Students often think an agent understands its task. Give them a small gridworld and let them design the reward themselves. Then show them what their agent actually learned, and let them fix the reward.
Quick check! With a discount of zero point five, what is a reward of eight, arriving in three steps, worth now?
One: zero point five cubed is one eighth, and one eighth of eight is one. A low discount makes the agent short-sighted.

In the app, open the agent loop lab. Watch Darsi Tiny take a request one step at a time: its plan, the tool call, the result and its answer. Then name its PEAS: its performance measure, environment, actuators and sensors.
Your turn. Which reward best stops the cleaning agent from dropping and re-collecting dirt?
Reward the state of the room, such as how clean it is, rather than each action. Remember: specify PEAS first, MDPs model sequential decisions, and the agent optimises exactly what you reward.

checkpoints.prompt: Discount 0.5. A reward of 8 in three steps is worth now:
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: multiply by 0.5 three times: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1.

checkpoints.prompt: Which reward best stops the drop-and-collect loop?

options.text: Reward how clean the room is

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: reward the outcome, not the action.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: rewarding pickups is what created the loop.
